The pruned church cannot afford that and should not want to. It has to be a place where doubt is spoken without being punished, where the questions the culture asks are asked inside the church and answered with more than slogans, where a man can bring his unbelief and not be shamed for it. "I believe; help my unbelief!" (Mark 9:24) is a prayer Jesus honored — he did not lecture the man on the contradiction in it, he healed his son — and a church that cannot hold that prayer cannot reach the people the decline has produced. Honesty about doubt is not a weakening of the witness. It is the precondition for any witness the skeptic will believe, because the skeptic can smell a church that is performing certainty it does not feel, and that smell sends him out the door faster than any argument.

Notice the order Jesus put these in his own ministry, because the order is the antidote to our anxiety about results. He did not begin by gathering a crowd and then disciple whoever was left. He began with the few, with the twelve, with the deep slow forming of a handful, and the crowd was a byproduct that came and went and was never the point. We have inverted it. We try to gather the crowd first and disciple it second, and we find, every time, that you cannot disciple a crowd, that the crowd disperses the moment the cost appears, that the energy we spent gathering it was energy stolen from the few we could actually have formed. The pruned church is being forced back into Jesus' order — the few first, deeply, and the rest left to God — and the forcing is a mercy, because Jesus' order is the only one that ever produced anything that lasted. The man who tries to disciple a thousand will disciple no one. The man who pours himself into three may, in time, see those three pour themselves into nine, and the nine into twenty-seven, in the slow geometric multiplication that built the whole church before anyone invented a strategy for it. Depth is not slower than breadth. It only looks slower, because its results are hidden and delayed, where breadth produces a crowd you can photograph this Sunday. But the crowd you photographed this Sunday is gone next Sunday, and the three you discipled this year are still following Christ in twenty, and have made others who will follow him in forty, long after the photographed crowd has scattered to the wind.

The fourth mark is mercy that costs something. The early church grew because it cared for the sick and the exposed and the poor at real cost to itself, and that cruciform mercy was the witness. The pruned church, stripped of its cultural power, has nothing left to offer the world but love, which turns out to be the only thing the world was ever going to believe. A small church that genuinely cares for the widow, the addict, the prisoner, the dying — that spends its reduced resources on people who can do nothing for it in return — bears the exact fruit Jesus named, the laying down of life for friends. This mercy will not fill the building. The addict you walk through recovery will not tithe; he may relapse and break your heart twice before he ever sits through a service. The dying widow you visit weekly for two years will be dead at the end of it, and she will not have brought a single new family in. The mercy does not pencil out. It is the fruit anyway, and the church that measures it by whether it grows the attendance has not understood that the mercy is the point and the attendance was never the point.

Before the fifth mark, let me dwell on the household a little more, because it is the one most foreign to how we have done church for a century and therefore the one most likely to be skipped. We built a model in which the home was where you slept and the church building was where faith happened, and we trained Christians to think of formation as something that occurs in a building, led by professionals, on a schedule, in programs designed for age-segregated groups — the children over here, the teenagers over there, the adults in the sanctuary, everyone formed apart from everyone else. And the household, the actual place where life is shared across generations, became almost irrelevant to the church's idea of discipleship, a place to recover from the week rather than the place where faith is made. The early church would not have understood this. For them the household was the church — they met in homes, ate in homes, were taught in homes, and the faith was passed down the way everything important is passed down, around tables, between generations, in the ordinary sharing of life. The pruned church, unable to sustain the building-and-program model, is being pushed back toward the household, and the parents who have been outsourcing their children's faith to the youth program are discovering that the youth program is gone or shrinking and the formation is now theirs, and this terrifies them, and it should not, because it is a return to the only model that ever reliably worked. Faith has always been transmitted best in households — not perfectly, never perfectly, but better there than anywhere else, because the household is where the child sees the faith lived when no one is performing, sees the parent pray and forgive and fail and repent, sees, in the texture of ordinary days, what it actually looks like to follow Christ. The building could never show that. The program could never show that. Only the household could, and the church spent a century moving away from it, and the decline is moving us back, and the moving-back is not a defeat. It is the recovery of the church's oldest and best classroom, the table, where the faith was handed down before there were any buildings at all.

There is a kind of honest preaching that the pruned church can recover, and I want to commend it as part of the third mark, because doubt and honest preaching are joined. The Christendom preacher, needing to keep everyone, learned to preach a Scripture with the hard parts sanded off — the wrath, the cost, the texts that offend, the demands that cut against the culture. He preached the comforting verses and skipped the uncomfortable ones, and over time his people received a Bible that had been quietly edited down to what would not lose them, a gospel with the offense removed. The pruned church, having already lost the people the offense would have driven away, can preach the whole counsel of God again — the hard texts with the soft ones, the wrath with the mercy, the cost with the comfort — because it is no longer protecting a crowd that the truth might thin. And the strange thing is that the whole Bible, preached honestly, reaches the doubter in a way the edited one never could, because the doubter can tell when he is being handled, when the preacher is steering around the hard parts to keep the room comfortable, and that steering reads to him as dishonesty, as a man who does not believe his own book enough to preach the difficult half of it. The preacher who works the hard texts, who does not flinch from the parts the culture hates, who lets the Bible be as strange and demanding as it actually is — that preacher the doubter can respect, even when he disagrees, because at least the man is dealing with the real thing and not a sanded-down version designed to offend no one. Honest preaching of the whole Scripture is itself a fruit of the pruning, made possible by the loss of the crowd that the dishonesty was protecting.

The fifth mark is worship that is for God and not for the crowd. When the church chased the crowd, worship became a product calibrated to an audience, and the question quietly shifted from "is this true and reverent" to "will this fill the room." The pruned church, having lost the crowd, can stop performing for it. It can worship as if God is the only audience, because increasingly he is the only one left, and that recovery — worship as the offering of a people to God rather than a service delivered to consumers — is itself a fruit. The smaller room can hold a deeper reverence, because there is no longer a crowd to entertain, only a God to worship. There is something that happens in a room of forty people who are genuinely worshiping, who are not performing and not being performed at, that a thousand-seat production engineered for excitement cannot touch, and the decline is handing that back to us if we will receive it instead of mourning the production we lost.

There is a sixth mark I almost left off because it is the least comfortable, and leaving it off would have been cowardice, so here it is: the willingness to tell the truth even when the truth empties the room. The Christendom church learned, over centuries of needing to keep everyone, to file down the hard edges of the gospel until it offended no one, because offending people meant losing them and losing them meant a smaller church and a smaller church meant failure. So the preaching got soft, not heretical exactly, just careful, just safe, just calibrated to keep the maximum number of people minimally comfortable. The pruned church, having already lost the crowd, is freed from that calculation. It can say the hard thing — about sin, about the cost of following Christ, about the things the culture insists on and the gospel forbids, about the things the church got wrong and needs to repent of — because it is no longer protecting a fullness it has already lost. Jesus emptied his own room on purpose more than once. In John 6, after the crowd had eaten the loaves and wanted to make him king, he gave them a teaching so hard that most of them walked away, and he turned to the twelve and asked, "Do you want to go away as well?" (John 6:67). He did not chase the departing crowd. He did not soften the teaching to keep them. He let them go, and kept the few who stayed for the truth, and the few were the church. A pruned church can preach like that, can let the people who only ever wanted the loaves go, can keep the few who stay for the bread of life, because it has nothing left to lose by telling the truth and everything to lose by continuing to hide it.

Now I have to say the hard thing about all five of these, because the church will immediately try to turn them into a growth strategy, and the moment it does they die. These are not techniques. If you take up depth and household and honesty and mercy and worship in order to fill the room, you have made them into franchise tools and they will produce nothing, because Jesus did not say "bear fruit and you will abide." He said "abide and you will bear fruit." The order is fixed and it cannot be reversed. The fruit is the byproduct of the abiding, never the goal pursued directly, and the church that pursues the fruit while skipping the abiding gets neither. I have watched churches read a list like this one and immediately ask, "Yes, but will it work? Will it grow us?" — and that question, the moment it is asked, has already poisoned the whole thing, because it has made the love and the mercy and the worship into means to an end, and Christ refuses to be reached as a means to an end. Every one of these marks is simply what abiding looks like when it is real. They are the shape a connected branch takes, not a method for becoming connected.

I have to indict myself one final time on this point, because it is the sin I am most prone to. I have taken genuinely good things — discipleship, mercy, honest preaching — and quietly bent them toward the goal of growth, asking of each one whether it would bring people in, which is to say corrupting the fruit by pursuing it directly. I started a mercy ministry once and caught myself, six months in, more interested in whether it was raising our profile in the community than in whether it was actually loving anyone, and I had to repent of having used the poor as a marketing department for my church's reputation. I have skipped the abiding and gone straight for the fruit, and gotten the predictable nothing, and blamed the culture for the emptiness my own disordered aim produced. I did this. The pruned church's hardest discipline is to do these things for their own sake, as the overflow of a life joined to Christ, and to refuse — actively, daily, against every instinct — to ask whether they are working, because the question "is it working" has already replaced God with the metric.

Let me put one more scene to this, because the abiding-before-fruit order is the hardest thing in the book to actually live, and a scene helps more than an argument. There was a season in our church when, having read enough of the right books, we decided to "do discipleship." We launched the groups, set the curriculum, recruited the leaders, tracked the participation. And it produced almost nothing, and I could not figure out why, because we were doing all the right things. It took me an embarrassingly long time to see it: we had taken up discipleship as a program to grow the church, and everyone could feel it, including the people in the groups, who sensed that they were being processed rather than loved, moved through a system rather than known. We had reached for the fruit and skipped the abiding. The discipleship was real activity aimed at a result, not the overflow of a people genuinely joined to Christ and therefore genuinely joined to each other. When it finally started to bear fruit — years later, after I had given up on it as a strategy — it was because a few people simply started actually following Jesus together, eating together, praying together, telling each other the truth, with no eye on whether it grew the church, and the thing we had failed to manufacture as a program grew up on its own as the natural shape of people who were actually abiding. The order is fixed. You cannot reach the fruit by aiming at the fruit. You reach the fruit by abiding, and the fruit comes when you have stopped watching for it, the way a vine does not strain to produce grapes; it stays joined to the root, and the grapes are simply what a joined branch eventually does.

These are not techniques for filling the room. They are the shape of abiding. Do them because you are joined to the vine and this is what joined branches do, and leave the question of fruit, and of fullness, and of the future, to the Vinedresser, who has never yet failed to bring a harvest from a branch that stayed connected to the source through the winter of its cutting. Do them whether they work or not. Do them especially when they do not seem to be working, because that is precisely when you find out whether you were abiding or merely strategizing, and the finding out, painful as it is, is itself part of the fruit.
chapters.verdict: These are not techniques for filling the room. They are the shape of abiding.
reflect: Which of these marks is most absent in your church, and why?
Where has your church pursued the fruit by skipping the abiding?
What would you stop doing if you stopped measuring by attendance?

chapters.title: Raising Children in the Ruins
chapters.summary: The hardest question for parents and pastors in a declining church is how to pass on a faith that the culture no longer reinforces. This chapter addresses handing the faith to the next generation without the scaffolding of Christendom, drawing on the author's own fatherlessness and five sons.
chapters.body:
There is a fear that lives underneath the church's fear about its own survival, and it is a more personal fear, the one that wakes parents at night: what about the kids? It is one thing to accept that the church I grew up in is passing. It is another thing entirely to watch my own children grow up in a world that gives them no reason to believe, no cultural current carrying them toward faith, no peer group that assumes it, no school that reinforces it, nothing but the open question and a thousand voices answering it the other way. The Christendom parent could outsource a good deal of the faith's transmission to the surrounding culture. The post-Christendom parent cannot outsource any of it. And that terrifies people, and it should, and I want to talk about it honestly because I have five sons and I have lain awake about it like everyone else.

Let me start with the loss, because it is real and pretending otherwise helps no one. My parents' generation, and to a lesser extent my own, could count on a great deal of help in raising believing children. The culture did half the work. The schools assumed it. The neighbors reinforced it. Sunday was protected; the whole town slowed down for it. A kid absorbed a basic Christian moral vocabulary from the air, from television even, from the simple fact that nearly everyone around him was at least nominally on the same page. The faith did not have to be installed deliberately and defended constantly, because it was the water, and the kids swam in it whether their parents were diligent or not. That help is gone. It is not coming back in our lifetimes. The parent today who assumes the culture will do any of the work of forming a believer is going to wake up one day to a child who absorbed the actual water he was swimming in — a water of consumerism and self-invention and the absolute authority of personal feeling — and wonder where the faith went. It went where it always goes when no one passes it on deliberately. It evaporated, replaced by whatever the actual culture was teaching while we assumed the old culture still was.

I want to be specific about what the actual water is now, because we keep using the word "secular" as though the culture were teaching our children nothing, a kind of neutral absence of faith, and that is dangerously wrong. The culture is not neutral. It is catechizing our children every waking hour, with more repetition and more skill and more emotional force than the church ever managed, and it is teaching them a coherent rival gospel that they absorb the way I absorbed Christianity in the old days — from the water, without ever being asked whether they believe it. The rival gospel goes something like this: you are the author of your own meaning; your feelings are the most reliable guide to truth; the purpose of life is to discover and express your authentic self; anything that constrains that self-expression is oppression; happiness is the highest good and suffering is meaningless and to be avoided; and you are accountable, finally, to no one but yourself. Our children are being discipled into that creed every time they pick up a phone, and it is not presented as an argument they could weigh and reject; it is presented as the water, the obvious, the assumed, the air. So the parent who thinks the choice is between giving the child faith and giving the child nothing has misread the situation entirely. The choice is between two faiths, two catechisms, two waters, and if the parent does not deliberately and powerfully form the child in the gospel of Christ, the child will be formed, automatically and thoroughly, in the gospel of the self, because something is always doing the forming and the culture never takes a day off. This raises the stakes and it also clarifies them. We are not trying to add a little religion to a neutral child. We are in a contest for the deepest loyalties of a soul that some very effective rival is already discipling, and the only way to win a contest like that is with a faith more compelling, more lived, more costly and more beautiful than the cheap creed the culture is selling — which means a lukewarm cultural Christianity will lose, every time, to a culture that believes its own gospel with far more conviction than the lukewarm church believes its.

So the first thing to say is that the scaffolding is gone and it is not coming back, and the sooner parents and pastors accept that, the sooner we can stop waiting for the schools and the neighbors and the broader culture to do our job. They will not. The job is ours now, undelegated and undeniable, and that is frightening, and it is also, I have come to think, a mercy in disguise, because the scaffolding was always doing something to the faith that we did not notice while we leaned on it. It was producing exactly the nominal, inherited, cost-free faith that the decline is now exposing as hollow. The kids who "absorbed" Christianity from the culture mostly absorbed a cultural Christianity that fell off the moment the culture stopped reinforcing it — which is precisely what we are watching happen to a whole generation. The scaffolding never built strong faith. It built convenient faith, and convenient faith does not survive a hard wind, and a hard wind has come.

Here is the strange hope buried in that. The faith we are now forced to hand our children deliberately, against the culture, at cost — that faith has a chance to be the real thing in a way the inherited version rarely was. A child who comes to believe in a world that gives him every reason not to, who chooses the faith knowing it will mark him as strange among his peers, who holds it against the current rather than floating along with it — that child has a faith worth more than a whole generation of cultural Christians, because his faith was never propped up by anything external and therefore has nothing external to lose. We cannot give our children the Christendom we had. We can give them something better: a faith that knows, from the beginning, that it is a costly allegiance and not a cultural default. That is closer to the New Testament. The first Christians raised their children as a tiny minority in a hostile empire, and they handed down a faith that conquered that empire, and they did it without a single Christian school or Christian neighbor or protected Sunday. It can be done. It has been done. It is, in fact, the normal condition of the faith across most of history; ours was the strange and comfortable exception.

But it has to be done deliberately, and this is where I have to get specific and personal, because I am not handing you a theory. I came to faith out of atheism, as a young man, with no Christian formation behind me at all and no father in front of me to model anything. I was raised without a father, and I have written elsewhere about what that does to a boy, the hole it leaves, the way it shapes everything afterward whether you want it to or not. So when I had sons of my own — five of them — I had no template. I could not raise them the way my father raised me, because my father was not there. I had to build the formation from nothing, deliberately, on purpose, with no cultural current to help and no inherited pattern to copy. And what I learned in doing that is, I think, exactly what the post-Christendom church now has to learn, because my situation as a fatherless atheist building a Christian household from scratch is becoming everyone's situation: we are all building it from scratch now, without the scaffolding, on purpose or not at all.

What does deliberate formation actually look like? It looks, first, like the table. We eat together, and at the table the faith gets talked about the way real things get talked about — not lectured, not performed, but woven into the ordinary conversation about the day, the news, the fight one of the boys had with a friend, the question one of them brought home from school. The faith is not a subject we cover on Sundays. It is the air in the house, but a deliberate air now, an air we keep breathing into the room on purpose because the wider world will not supply it. We pray before we are fully awake and before we sleep and over the food and in the car when something hard happens, not as a performance but because that is how people who actually believe behave, and children learn what is real by watching what their parents do when they think the formal religious moment is over.

I want to say a word about the danger of overcorrecting, because I have watched earnest parents, terrified of the culture, try to seal their children off from it entirely — to build a fortress, to control every input, to keep the child so thoroughly inside the Christian bubble that the rival gospel never reaches him. And I understand the impulse, God knows I have felt it with five sons, but I have come to think the fortress strategy fails, and fails predictably, because the child raised in a sealed fortress eventually leaves the fortress, as all children do, and meets the world with no antibodies of his own, having never been allowed to encounter a hard question inside the safety of home, and the world, which has been waiting, takes him apart. The fortress does not produce strong faith; it produces brittle faith, faith that has never been tested and therefore shatters at the first real test, which comes the moment the child is out of the parents' control. What produces strong faith is not the fortress but the inoculation — letting the child encounter the hard questions and the rival claims while still at home, while there is a believing parent to talk it through with, so that the faith is tested in safety and grows the antibodies it will need when the test comes for real. My sons are going to meet the rival gospel; I cannot prevent it and I have stopped trying. What I can do is make sure they meet it first at my table, where they can ask me the hard thing and get an honest answer, rather than first in a dorm room, where they will get the rival gospel's answer and no other. The goal is not a child who never encountered doubt. It is a child who encountered doubt early, at home, with help, and came through it with a faith that is his own because it was tested and held.

It looks, second, like honesty about the cost and the doubt. I have never pretended to my sons that the faith is easy or that I have no questions. I came to it through doubt; I am not going to forbid them the road I traveled. When one of them brings me the hard question — why does God allow this, how do we know any of it is true, why should I believe what my friends all think is a fairy tale — I do not panic and I do not shut it down, because I remember being the kid asking those questions and getting shut down, and the shutting down is what nearly cost me the faith forever. I take the question seriously. I tell him what I actually think, and where I am not sure, and how I came to believe it anyway. A child who is allowed to doubt out loud in a believing home has somewhere to bring the doubt. A child who learns that doubt is forbidden takes it underground, and underground is where faith goes to die.

It looks, third, like preparing them to be a minority, which is the thing my generation was never prepared for and theirs cannot avoid. I am raising my sons to expect that the world will think them strange, that holding this faith will cost them socially, that they will be the odd ones, the ones who do not go along, and that this is not a sign something has gone wrong but exactly what was promised. The early church catechized its children for a hostile world. We catechized ours for a friendly one, and then the world turned, and a generation walked into the cold without a coat. I am trying to send my sons out with a coat — with the expectation of cost built in from the start, so that when the cost comes it confirms their faith instead of shattering it. "Do not be surprised, brothers, that the world hates you" (1 John 3:13). I want that to be old news to my sons by the time the world gets around to demonstrating it.

It looks, fourth, like letting them see the faith cost you something, which may be the most important of all and the hardest to fake. Children are unerring detectors of what is real. They can tell the difference between a faith their parents perform on Sundays and a faith their parents actually live, and the difference shows up not in the religious moments but in the ordinary ones — in how the parent handles money, treats the person who can do nothing for him, responds to being wronged, behaves when the diagnosis is bad and the prayer seems unanswered. A child who watches his father forgive someone who hurt the family, really forgive, at real cost, learns more about the gospel than a hundred lessons could teach, because he has seen the thing operate on his father where it was expensive. A child who watches his parents give away money they could have spent on him, for the sake of someone in need, learns that this faith is not free and not theoretical. The faith that transmits is the faith that visibly costs the people transmitting it. The faith that is cheap for the parents — that never seems to require anything, never produces a hard choice, never shows up where it would hurt — that faith does not transmit, because the child correctly reads it as decoration, as a hobby, as the thing the family does on Sundays that has no bearing on the things the family does the rest of the week. I want my sons to see the faith cost me, not because I am performing martyrdom for them, but because if it does not cost me anything then I am not actually living it, and they will know, and they will rightly conclude it is not worth their own cost either.

I have to confess the fear has not left me even as I write this. I do not know how it comes out for my boys. No parent does, and the parent who tells you he has guaranteed his children's faith by his method is selling you the same lie the church told itself about the scaffolding. I cannot guarantee them anything. I can only hand them the faith as honestly and deliberately and tenderly as I know how, build the household the wider world will not build, refuse to outsource what is mine to do, and then release them to the same God who reached me when I was a fatherless atheist with no business ever believing anything. He reached me without any scaffolding at all. He found me in the ruins, before there were any ruins to speak of in the wider culture, when I was my own private ruin. If he can do that, he can find my sons in whatever ruins they grow up in, and the most important thing I can hand them is not a sealed-up faith but a true picture of the God who specializes in finding people exactly where I was found.

I have to say something to the parents whose children have already walked away, because some of you are reading this with a particular ache that the rest of the chapter does not touch, and I will not pretend you are not in the room. You did everything I have described. You built the household. You were honest about doubt. You let them see the faith cost you. And they walked away anyway — into the indifference, into the antibodies, into a culture that gave them a thousand reasons to leave and you only the truth, and the truth did not hold them, or has not held them yet. And you are carrying a grief and a guilt that no parenting method can address, because the methods all imply that if you do it right the children stay, and yours did not, and so you conclude you did it wrong, that it is your fault, that you failed at the one thing that mattered most. Hear me. The transmission of faith is not a machine where the right inputs guarantee the right outputs. It cannot be, because faith is finally a gift of God and a free response of a person, and a person, even your beloved child, remains free, which means even the best formation can be refused. God himself, the perfect Father, raised children in a perfect garden and watched them walk away. If the perfect Father, with perfect formation, in a perfect environment, had children who left, then the departure of a child is not proof of a parent's failure. Keep the door open. Keep loving them without conditions. Keep praying, because the God who reached me as a grown atheist who had walked further from him than your child has reaches grown prodigals all the time, and the story is not over while they are still breathing. I came to faith as an adult, out of nothing, against my own pride, and the people who get to me were not my parents, because I did not have the parents for it. God found me anyway. He can find your child anyway. Your job was never to guarantee the outcome. It was to hand on the faith as faithfully as you could and then entrust the child to the only One who can finally save him, which is the same thing you have to do whether the child stays or leaves: let go of the outcome into the hands of God, and refuse to let your grief curdle into the lie that it was all for nothing.

We cannot give our children the culture we had. That culture is gone, and grieving it will not bring it back, and clinging to its corpse will only teach our children that our faith was mostly about the culture, which is the worst lesson we could possibly teach them. But we can give them the only thing that ever mattered in that culture, the thing the culture mostly obscured — the living God who was never the same thing as the Christian society that surrounded us, who was always underneath it and behind it and beyond it, and who is still here, still finding people, still reaching into ruins after the exact kind of person everyone had written off. That is what I am trying to hand my sons. Not the water that drained away. The vine the water was never the source of in the first place.
chapters.verdict: We cannot give our children the culture we had, but we can give them the only thing that ever mattered in it.
reflect: What faith are you handing your children — a cultural habit or a costly allegiance?
Where are you relying on the culture to do the formation that belongs to you?
What would it mean to prepare your children to be a minority?

chapters.title: The Pastor in the Winter
chapters.summary: The decline takes a specific and brutal toll on those who lead, and the temptation to despair, to perform, or to flee is acute. This chapter speaks directly to pastors and leaders, naming the particular grief of leading a shrinking flock and the spiritual disciplines that sustain a shepherd in a long winter.
chapters.body:
I want to talk to the pastors now, and the elders, and the deacons, and the worn-out volunteers who have held a ministry together with their own two hands for longer than anyone thanked them for. The rest of you are welcome to listen, and you should, because you ought to know what the long winter is doing to the people you have asked to lead you through it. But this chapter is for the ones at the front, because the decline does something to the shepherd that it does not quite do to the sheep, and almost nobody talks about it, and it is killing good men and women in slow motion, and I have felt enough of it myself to recognize the symptoms in everyone I sit across the table from at the pastors' gatherings.

Here is what the decline does to a pastor. It attacks the place where his identity and his work have fused, and for most of us that fusion runs deeper than we ever admitted while things were going well. When the church was full, I told myself my identity was in Christ, and I believed it, and I was largely lying without knowing it, because the test of where your identity actually lives is what happens to your soul when the thing is taken away. And when the numbers fell, I found out. The falling numbers did not just discourage me. They indicted me. They felt like a verdict on my worth as a man, because somewhere along the way the size of my church had become the measure of my significance, and I had not noticed the substitution because the church kept growing and so the idol kept paying out. The decline stopped the payments, and only then did I discover how much of my sense of being a worthwhile person had been riding on a number I do not control and was never supposed to be serving in the first place.

That is the first thing the winter does: it exposes whose approval you have actually been serving. We say we serve God. We say it sincerely. But watch what happens to a pastor when the attendance drops, and you will see whose approval was really running him. If a falling number can crush a man, then the number was his god, whatever he professed on Sunday, because only your god can crush you by withdrawing. The decline is performing an excruciating mercy on pastors: it is smashing the idol of the metric, and the smashing feels like the destruction of the man, because the man had grown around the idol like a tree around a fence post, and you cannot pull the post without tearing the wood. But the wood needs the post pulled. A pastor whose worth depends on his attendance is a pastor who will eventually sacrifice the gospel to the attendance, because he has to feed the thing his soul is living on, and the decline is, brutally, graciously, starving that out of us.

Before I name the exits, let me describe the particular loneliness of it, because the loneliness is the soil all three exits grow in. The pastor in a declining church is lonely in a way that is hard to explain to people who have not carried it. He cannot tell the congregation how worried he is, because his worry would frighten them and they look to him for hope. He often cannot tell the denomination, because the denomination is measuring him and worry reads as failure. He frequently cannot tell his fellow pastors, because the culture of ministry has trained men to present the highlight reel, to answer "how's the church?" with "God's doing great things," even when the church is dying and God seems silent, because admitting otherwise feels like admitting personal defeat. So he carries it alone. He stands up Sunday after Sunday and projects a confidence he does not feel to a room that is slowly emptying, and then he goes home and the mask comes off and there is no one there who knows the weight of what he just performed. That loneliness is corrosive. It is the specific occupational hazard of the shepherd, and it is worse in the winter than at any other time, because in the summer at least the visible success masks the loneliness, and in the winter the loneliness stands fully exposed with nothing to distract from it.

The second thing the winter does is present three exits, and all three are deadly, and most of us try at least two of them before we find the narrow way through. The first exit is despair — to give up inwardly, to keep going through the motions while the hope dies, to become a chaplain to a dying institution who has privately written the obituary and is just waiting out the clock. I have been close enough to that exit to feel the cold air coming off it. The second exit is performance — to throw everything into manufacturing the appearance of life, the new programs, the better production, the relentless positivity, the frantic activity that is really just a man running from the silence because the silence might tell him the truth. The performing pastor looks like the opposite of the despairing one, but they are twins; both have stopped trusting God with the outcome and started managing the appearance, one by giving up and one by frantically pretending. The third exit is flight — the new church, the better call, the escape to a context where the numbers are still good and the idol can keep paying out, dressed up, always, in the language of God's leading. Sometimes a move really is God's leading. But I have watched too many men flee a hard winter for a greener pasture and carry the exact same idol into the new field, where it will demand the same sacrifices and eventually fail them the same way, because the problem was never the field.

The narrow way through is none of the three, and it is harder than all of them, and it is this: to let the winter do its work on your own soul first, before you ask what it is doing to your church. The pruning is not only happening to the congregation. It is happening to the pastor, and the cuts the Vinedresser is making in you — the cutting away of your need for the crowd, your fusion of identity and attendance, your service of an idol you called ministry — those cuts are the most important thing happening in your church right now, more important than any strategy, because a shepherd who has been pruned of his idols can lead a flock through a winter, and a shepherd still feeding the metric will lead them in circles around his own anxiety until they are as lost as he is.

So what sustains a shepherd through the long winter? Let me be practical, because piety in the abstract has never warmed anyone on a cold Tuesday.

I want to say something to the lay leaders too, the elders and deacons and the volunteers, because the chapter has leaned toward the paid pastor and the winter falls just as hard on the unpaid faithful, sometimes harder. There is a particular weariness that belongs to the lay leader in a declining church — the woman who has run the children's ministry for twenty years and now has four children to teach where she once had forty, the man who has been an elder through three pastors and watched each of them leave, the volunteers who keep the building open and the lights on and the doors open because if they stop, no one will. These people do not have the theological framework the pastor has, the books, the language for what is happening. They just have the fatigue, and the love, and the slow grinding question of whether it is worth it to keep coming back to a ministry that keeps shrinking. To them I want to say what is hardest for them to hear, because they are the least thanked people in the church: your faithfulness is seen. Not by the crowd, which is gone, and often not even by the pastor, who is drowning in his own version of the winter and forgets to thank you. But it is seen by the One who sees in secret, and it is counted, every Sunday you open the door for four children, every year you keep teaching the dwindling class, every quiet act of keeping the lights on that no one notices and no one celebrates. You are not maintaining a failure. You are tending a remnant, keeping a flame alive through a long dark, and the keeping of a flame through the dark is among the most honored works in the whole economy of God, however little it is honored among us. Do not measure your faithfulness by the size of the class. Measure it by the faithfulness itself, which is complete in four children as fully as in forty, because the four are souls and a soul is not less of a soul for being one of few.

First, a daily reckoning with the audience of One. Every morning, before the numbers can get to you, you have to relocate your worth back to where it belongs, deliberately, because it will not stay there on its own; it drifts back to the metric the way water finds the lowest point. The reckoning is simple and it is brutal: I am not the size of my church. I am a man Christ died for and called and will keep, and if this church closes tomorrow that fact does not move an inch. You have to preach that to yourself before you preach anything to anyone else, and most days you will not feel it, and you preach it anyway, because feeling follows obedience more often than it leads it.

Second, brothers. Do not winter alone. The reason I can write this chapter is that I have sat across enough tables from enough pastors in enough diners to know that the isolation is the killer — that the shame of a shrinking church drives men into hiding precisely when they most need to be seen, and the hiding is where the despair and the performance and the flight all incubate. Find the other shepherds in the winter. Tell them the true number and the true state of your soul. Let them tell you theirs. This is half of why the Pastors Connection Network exists, if I am honest about it: not to share growth strategies but to keep men alive through the winter by refusing to let them face it alone, because a pastor who can say the true thing out loud to one other man who will not flinch is a pastor who can survive almost anything, and a pastor who carries it all in silence is a pastor on his way to one of the three exits whether he knows it yet or not.

Let me name something about Sabbath and rest specifically, because the pastor in the winter is uniquely prone to abandon it, and abandoning it is how the winter kills him. When the numbers are falling, the temptation is to work harder, longer, more frantically, to try to outwork the decline, to fill the empty hours with activity in the hope that activity will reverse the trend. It will not. But the pastor, panicked, drops his day off, drops his prayer, drops the rest that keeps him human, and pours the recovered hours into a frantic effort that produces nothing but his own exhaustion. And the exhaustion is precisely what hands him to the three exits, because a rested man can resist despair and a depleted one cannot. The Sabbath is not a luxury the busy pastor cannot afford in a crisis. It is the discipline that keeps him alive through the crisis, the weekly insistence that the church does not depend on his frantic effort, that God runs the world while the pastor sleeps, that the outcome was never his to manufacture and so he can rest from trying. The pastor who keeps the Sabbath through the winter is making a confession every week, the confession that he is not the savior of his church, that he can stop, that the church is held by God and not by his ceaseless labor. The pastor who abandons the Sabbath is making the opposite confession, that it all depends on him, that he cannot rest because if he stops the whole thing falls — which is functional atheism dressed as dedication, and it will burn him to the ground, slowly, while he congratulates himself on his commitment.

Third, the long obedience in the hidden work. When the visible fruit is gone, you have to learn to find your sustenance in the work that only God sees, or you will starve, because the public fruit that used to feed you has been withdrawn. The visit to the dying saint. The hour over the text. The teenager you are slowly winning. The marriage you are quietly holding together in the counseling room. None of it shows up anywhere. All of it is the actual work, the work that was always the work, that the full building let you neglect because the building itself looked like fruit. The winter strips away the appearance of fruit and leaves you with the real fruit, which was always hidden, and the discipline is to learn to be fed by the hidden thing, because "your Father who sees in secret" is the only audience that was ever real, and the winter is teaching you, the hard way, to work for him alone.

Fourth, and I almost did not include this because it sounds too simple to be a discipline, you have to learn to receive ministry and not only give it. The pastor in the winter is uniquely tempted to become a man who pours out and never takes in, who is everyone's shepherd and no one's sheep, who has no one pastoring him because he is the pastor and pastors are supposed to be the strong ones. That is a recipe for a dry well and then a dead man. Even Jesus, who needed nothing from anyone in the way we need things, withdrew to be alone with the Father, let a woman anoint his feet, let his friends keep him company in his agony in the garden — and was disappointed when they fell asleep, which tells you he wanted them there. If the Son of God let himself be ministered to, the pastor who refuses it is not being strong. He is being proud, and the pride will kill him slowly in the winter, because the winter takes more out of a man than the summer ever did and gives back less, and a man drawing down his reserves with nothing coming in will eventually hit the bottom. You have to let someone pastor you. Your wife, if she is willing and able to carry it, though be careful not to make her your only well, because that is too much weight for a marriage to bear alone. A friend. A counselor. A spiritual director, if you can find one. The other pastors in the network who know the winter from inside. Somebody has to be allowed to ask how your soul is and to wait for a true answer, because a shepherd who is starving cannot feed the flock, and the winter starves shepherds who will not be fed.

I have to tell you that I have failed at all of this, repeatedly, and that I write it as a fellow patient and not as a doctor who has recovered. I have despaired. I have performed. I have eyed the flight, and only the grace of God and a couple of stubborn friends who would not let me hide kept me from taking it for the wrong reasons. I have served the metric while preaching against it. I have come home from a thin Sunday and been short with my wife and my sons because a number had told me I was a failure and I believed the number over the gospel I had just preached. I did this. I am writing this chapter to myself as much as to you, and the only authority I have to write it is the authority of a man who has been wrong in all these ways and has felt, slowly, the Vinedresser cutting these very things out of him, and has learned that the cutting, though it felt like the end of him, was the beginning of the only kind of shepherd worth following into a winter.

I want to give the discouraged shepherd one image to hold, because images carry a man through a winter better than arguments do, and it is the image of the night shift. There is a kind of work that happens at night, in hospitals and on farms and in the homes of the dying, that no one sees and no one applauds and that is nonetheless the work that keeps the world running while everyone else sleeps. The nurse on the night shift is not less of a nurse because the corridors are dark and empty. She is doing the same work she would do at noon, and arguably harder work, with less recognition and less support, in the hours when the body and the spirit are weakest. The pastor in a declining church is on the night shift of the church's history. The lights are low. The applause is gone. The metrics that flatter the day-shift pastor — the full rooms, the growth, the buzz — are not available to you. But the work is the same work, and it is no less holy for being done in the dark, and it may be more holy, because it is being done without any of the rewards that might be confused for the reason. The day-shift pastor can never be entirely sure whether he serves God or the applause, because both are present. The night-shift pastor, with the applause withdrawn, finds out exactly whom he serves, because only one of them is still there at three in the morning. The winter is the night shift of the church, and the shepherd who keeps the watch through it — who does the unseen work, who tends the few, who stays awake while the world sleeps and the building empties — is not a failed day-shift pastor. He is doing the holiest version of the work there is, the version stripped of every reward but God himself, and God is watching the night shift more closely than he ever watched the crowded day.

The shepherd is not measured by the size of the flock but by his faithfulness to the One who owns it. The flock was never yours. The numbers were never the scoreboard. The Owner of the sheep will not ask you, on the last day, how many you gathered. He will ask whether you fed the ones he gave you, whether you stayed, whether you loved them when there was nothing in it for you, whether you kept your hand on the plow through the winter when no green thing was coming up. That is the whole job. It always was. The full building hid it, and the empty one has handed it back to you, and the handing back, painful as it is, may be the kindest thing the decline has done.
chapters.verdict: The shepherd is not measured by the size of the flock but by his faithfulness to the One who owns it.
reflect: Whose approval are you actually serving when you measure your ministry by numbers?
Where has your identity become fused with your church's size?
What sustains you on the Tuesday when nothing visible is happening?

chapters.title: What We Owe the Dying Church
chapters.summary: Some congregations will not survive, and the church needs a theology of dying well — how a congregation can end faithfully, what it owes the saints in its final years, and how a good death can itself be a witness and a seed.
chapters.body:
I have spent this whole book arguing against the assumption that decline means death, insisting on pruning and remnant and renewal and the long memory of a church that has buried empires. I believe all of it. And I would be a coward and a liar if I did not now turn and say the thing that all of it has been circling: some churches are going to die. Not be pruned. Die. The lampstand removed, the doors closed, the building sold, the congregation scattered, the name erased from the denominational rolls. It is happening by the thousands, and it is going to happen to some of the very churches reading this, and a book about decline that cannot speak honestly to the congregation that will not make it is a book that abandoned its hardest readers right when they needed it most. So I am going to speak to the dying church now, directly, without the consolation of pretending it is something else.

Here is the first thing, and it is the thing nobody says. A church can die well or a church can die badly, and the difference is enormous, and the difference is almost entirely within the congregation's control even when survival is not. We have no theology of dying well as a church, because we have spent so long treating survival as the only acceptable outcome that we have made congregational death unspeakable, and the unspeakable thing always gets handled worst. A church that cannot say out loud "we may not make it" cannot prepare to die faithfully, and so it dies the way people die who refused to admit they were dying — in denial, in panic, in a frantic clutching at survival that poisons the final years and leaves nothing behind but bitterness and an estate fight over the building. We need better than that. The saints in those final pews deserve better than that. And there is a better way to die, and the Scriptures know it, because the whole faith is built on a death that turned out to be the most fruitful event in the history of the world.

I learned a great deal about dying well, as it happens, from sitting with the actually dying, because the saints who died well taught me what a church dying well would look like. There was an old woman in one of my early churches, dying slowly of something that gave her months to know it was coming, and she did something with those months that I have never forgotten. She used them. She called people to her bedside and reconciled old hurts. She told her children and grandchildren the things she wanted them to carry. She gave away what she had, deliberately, to the people and causes she wanted it to serve, with her own hands while she could still see their faces. She blessed everyone she could reach. And she died, when she finally died, with nothing left undone and nothing left unsaid, having spent her dying as fully as she had spent her living, so that her death was not a defeat that happened to her but a final act of love that she performed. I have also sat with people who died the other way, clutching, terrified, denying it to the end, leaving everything unfinished and unsaid, dying as though death were an ambush rather than a thing they could meet with their eyes open. And the difference, every time, was whether they faced it in faith. The old woman could spend her dying so well because she was not afraid of what came after, because she knew who held her on the far side of the grave, and that knowledge freed her to give her death away instead of clinging to her life. A church can do the same, for the same reason. A congregation that knows its Lord conquered death can face its own death without terror, can spend its dying in blessing and reconciliation and generosity, can die the way that old woman died — not ambushed, but with its eyes open and its hands giving, performing in its death a final act of the love it lived.

Think about what makes a human death good or bad, because the same things apply to a church. A person can die badly — raging, terrified, clutching, denying to the end, making everyone around the deathbed miserable, leaving behind a mess of unfinished business and unforgiven wounds. Or a person can die well — at peace, having forgiven and been forgiven, having blessed the next generation, having handed on what they carried, leaving behind not a mess but an inheritance. We have all sat by both kinds of deathbed. I have, more than I can count, and I can tell you the difference is not whether the person was healthy or whether the death was fair. The difference is whether the dying was met with faith or with denial. The faithful death is the one that, knowing the end is coming, spends its last strength not on a doomed fight for more time but on the things that outlast time — reconciliation, blessing, the handing-on of the inheritance, the witness of a person who can face death without terror because they know who holds them on the other side of it.

A church can do exactly that. A dying congregation can spend its final years in one of two ways, and the choice is the whole of its faithfulness. It can spend them clutching — pouring its last money and its last energy into the desperate maintenance of a building it cannot fill, fighting over who is to blame, turning inward, growing bitter, dying the way a miser dies, with its fists closed around the very things it is about to lose anyway. Or it can spend them planting — using its final strength, its building, its endowment, its remaining people, to seed something beyond itself, to bless the next thing, to die the way a seed dies, with its hands open, scattering what it has where it might grow after the dying church is gone. "Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit" (John 12:24). That is the verse for the dying church, and it is the only one that turns the dying into something other than waste.

Let me make it concrete, because "die well" is a sentiment until it touches the actual decisions a dying church faces. A congregation that has accepted it will not survive can do extraordinary things with its death that it could never do with its survival. It can give its building to a younger congregation, a church plant, an immigrant fellowship meeting in a school cafeteria with nowhere permanent to go — and watch its sanctuary fill again with worship in a language the founders never spoke, which is not the death of the church on that corner but its resurrection in a form the founders could not have imagined. It can take its endowment, the money it was hoarding against a survival that is not coming, and pour it into missions, into church plants, into the training of young pastors, into the very seeds that will outlive it. It can spend its final years not in self-preservation but in radical, joyful generosity, giving itself away because it has finally understood that it cannot keep itself anyway, and that the only question left is whether its death will plant or only rot. The congregation that dies clutching leaves a sold building and a fight. The congregation that dies planting leaves a harvest it will not live to see, which is exactly what its Lord did.

There is a discernment buried in all this that the dying church most needs and least possesses, and it is the discernment between a building and a church, because the confusion of the two is what makes congregational death so much worse than it has to be. A building is not a church. A church is a people, joined to Christ and to each other, and a people can outlive a building, can leave a building, can give a building away and still be a church, because the church was never the building in the first place. But a dying congregation usually cannot tell the difference, because it has spent so many decades in the building that the building has become the church in its imagination, and so the loss of the building feels like the death of the church, when it may be only the death of an address. I have watched a congregation that could no longer sustain its building conclude that it therefore had to die — sell the building, scatter, end — when in fact it could have left the building, given it away, and continued as a church meeting in homes or in a borrowed room, smaller, freer, alive. They could not imagine it, because to them the building was the church, and so the death of the building was the death of everything, and they buried a living church because they could not separate it from its dying address. The discernment the dying church needs is exactly this: to ask whether what is dying is the people or only the property, the body or only the building, the church or only the place the church used to meet. Sometimes it really is the church that is dying — the people scattered, the love grown cold, the thing itself gone. But often it is only the building that is dying, and the people could go on, if they could only see that they were not the walls, that the church could walk out of the building and live, that the loss of the property is not the loss of the body unless the body has confused itself with the property. Tell the difference, and you may find that what looked like the death of a church is only the death of a building, and that the church, set free from the address that was draining it, can live.

And here is what I most want the dying church to hear, because the world will tell you the opposite and the world is wrong. A faithful death is not a failure. The congregation that ends well, that spends itself in blessing and dies with open hands, has not failed. It has done the most Christlike thing a church can do. It has laid down its life. We have so thoroughly equated survival with success that we have made faithful death look like the ultimate defeat, when in fact the founder of our faith achieved everything he achieved precisely by dying, and told us that the way of the cross is the way of life, and that the seed that refuses to fall into the ground and die is the seed that remains alone and fruitless. A church can save its life and lose it, clutching at survival until it rots. Or a church can lose its life and, in the losing, plant a harvest. The cross is not just the church's message. For some congregations, it is going to be the church's literal shape — death that bears fruit, an ending that turns out to be a seed.

There is something the dying church owes its own saints in those final years, and we almost never talk about it, so let me. A congregation in its last decade is full of old people who have given their whole lives to it — who were married in that sanctuary, who buried their parents from it, who taught the Sunday school and chaired the committees and kept the lights on through every previous hard time, who poured sixty years of love into a place that is now visibly dying around them. What does the church owe them? It owes them the truth, gently and in time, so that the ending does not ambush them. It owes them a death they can participate in rather than one that simply happens to them. And above all it owes them the assurance that their life's work was not wasted, because that is the fear that haunts the old saint in the dying church at three in the morning: that it was all for nothing, that the church she gave her life to is closing and therefore her life was spent on something that failed. The church owes her the truth that counters that fear, and the truth is this: the souls she loved into the kingdom are in the kingdom still. The children she taught are grown and scattered and carrying, some of them, a faith she planted. The kindness she showed for sixty years did its work in people whose names will never appear in any record. A church can close and its harvest still be standing, out in the world, in the people it formed, who walked out its doors and carried Christ into lives the church will never see. The building closing is not the harvest failing. The widow who gave her whole life to a church that is now dying did not waste it, and someone needs to look her in the eye in the final year and tell her so, with enough specificity that she can believe it, because she is going to need that truth to die in peace, and the church owes it to her.

I have to be careful here, because this can curdle into its own evasion, and I have watched it happen. There are churches that should fight to live and instead reach for the dignity of "dying well" as an excuse to stop trying, to avoid the hard work of change, to spiritualize their own giving-up. Not every church facing decline is a church facing death; I have spent twelve chapters insisting on that, and I will not undo it now. The call to die well is not a call to assume you are dying. It is a call for the church that genuinely is dying — that has discerned, honestly, before God, with counsel, that the end is actually coming — to meet that end with faith instead of denial. Discerning the difference between a church that should fight and a church that should plant is hard, and it belongs to the congregation and its leaders and God and wise outside counsel, not to a chapter in a book. But once that discernment has truly been made, once a church knows in its bones that the end is real, then the question is no longer how to survive. The question is how to die in a way that plants, and that question has a beautiful answer, and the dying church that asks it honestly may do more for the kingdom in its final three years than it did in its comfortable previous thirty.

I have buried churches, the way I have buried people. I have stood in the last service of a congregation, sung the last hymn in a building about to be sold, watched the saints weep over an ending that was real and would not be reframed away. And I have seen both kinds of death. I have seen a church die clutching, fighting over the building proceeds, the final years a misery, the last memory a lawsuit. And I have seen a church die planting — give its building to a young Hispanic congregation that had been meeting in a storefront, hand over the keys with tears and joy, attend the new church's first service in their old sanctuary, and walk out for the last time having watched their death become someone else's resurrection. The first church is a warning. The second church is a sermon, the loudest sermon it ever preached, the sermon of a body that finally believed its own gospel enough to lay itself down.

There is a grief in this that I do not want to rush past, even as I commend the planting death, because the people who have to make these decisions are not abstractions and the planting death is not painless just because it is faithful. To give your building to another congregation is to attend the last service in the room where you were married and your children were baptized and your parents were buried, and then to hand the keys to strangers and walk out for the last time. That is a death, a real one, and dressing it up as a "seed" does not make it hurt less in the moment of the handing-over. I have stood with congregations in that exact moment, and I have learned not to hurry them past the grief into the meaning. Let them weep in the empty sanctuary. Let them say goodbye to the room. Let the last service be a funeral, with all the grief a funeral carries, before it becomes a planting. The two are not opposites. The most fruitful deaths are the ones that were fully grieved and then fully given — grieved so the loss was honored, given so the loss could bear fruit. A church that skips the grief and rushes to the noble planting has not died well; it has performed a death while suppressing the feeling of one, and the suppressed grief will surface later as bitterness, even amid the apparent generosity. And a church that only grieves and never gives, that weeps in the sanctuary and then locks the doors and lets the building rot or sells it to the highest bidder and scatters the proceeds into nothing, has wasted the death entirely. The faithful death holds both, the way every faithful death does: the full weeping and the open hands, the funeral and the seed, the goodbye to the old room and the joy, real joy, of hearing it fill again with worship in a language the founders never knew. Grieve all the way down. Then give it all away. That is how a church dies the way its Lord died.

A church can die in a way that plants, or in a way that only rots. If your church is dying — really dying, honestly, after real discernment — then you still have a choice, the most important choice your congregation will ever make, more important than any choice it made in its years of strength. You can spend your death clutching, and leave a sold building and a bitter memory. Or you can spend it planting, with open hands, scattering everything you have where it might grow, dying the way your Lord died, which looked like the end of everything and turned out to be the seed of the world. Choose the planting. It is the last and maybe the truest fruit a pruned vine can bear — to fall into the ground, and die, and trust the Vinedresser to bring the harvest you will not be here to see.
chapters.verdict: A church can die in a way that plants, or in a way that only rots.
reflect: If your church does not survive, what do you want its last years to have been?
Where are you spending the church's final strength — on self-preservation or on faithfulness?
What might be planted by a death that is met with faith?

chapters.title: The Promise of Renewal
chapters.summary: The book closes by holding the tension it refuses to resolve: renewal is promised but not scheduled, certain but not controllable. The church is called to abide through a winter whose spring it cannot see, command, or guarantee.
chapters.body:
I will not end this book with a renewal you can schedule, because there is no such thing, and every book that promises one is lying to a frightened church for the price of its hope. The promise of renewal is real. It is also not in our hands, and not on our timeline, and the church has to learn to hold those two truths at once or it will collapse into either presumption or despair. Renewal is certain. Renewal is not controllable. Everything depends on the church's willingness to live inside that gap.

Begin with the certainty, because it is genuine and it is grounded in the character of God, not in the trend of the data. The Vinedresser cuts the vine he loves in order to bear more fruit, and a Vinedresser who only cut and never harvested would not be a vinedresser at all. The whole logic of the pruning is the coming crop. "He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ" (Philippians 1:6). The God who reduced the vine intends the harvest, and the resurrection is the permanent proof that in God's economy death is never the last word but the doorway, that the seed must fall into the ground and die before it bears, that the way to the empty tomb runs through the cross and not around it. A church that believes in the resurrection cannot finally believe in its own extinction, because the God it worships specializes in bringing life out of the place where life looked finished. The dry bones in Ezekiel's valley were not a little discouraged. They were bones — dry, scattered, bleached white in the sun, past any natural hope, the kind of dead that does not come back. And the word of the Lord came to them and they lived. "Can these bones live?" (Ezekiel 37:3). The prophet's answer is the only honest one for the declining church: "O Lord God, you know." Not "yes, here is the strategy." Not "no, it is hopeless." You know. The renewal is yours to give, and you have promised it, and I cannot command it.

I want to say something about hope as a discipline rather than a feeling, because everything in this book finally rests on a hope that the data does not supply, and I do not want to leave you thinking hope is a mood you either have or lack. It is not. Hope, the Christian kind, is not optimism and it is not a temperament and it is not a feeling that the sun will come out. It is a settled decision, renewed daily, to stake your life on the character of God against the evidence of your circumstances. It is a thing you do, not a thing you feel, and you do it most truly on the days you feel it least. I have practiced this hope at midnight with no feeling of hope whatsoever, simply by saying the true things out loud to a God I could not feel — that he is good, that he keeps his promises, that the cross and the empty tomb actually happened, that he has never yet failed his church and will not start with mine — and saying them not because they made me feel better, because often they did not, but because they were true and hope is the discipline of acting on the truth against the feeling. The branch in February does not feel the spring. It abides anyway, holding its connection to the vine through the cold, not because it has a warm feeling about April but because the connection is the truth and the cold is only the circumstance. That is hope. It is the branch holding on through a winter that gives it no evidence, on the strength of a connection it cannot feel, to a vine it cannot see flowing, trusting a spring it has no proof is coming. And the church is asked for exactly that hope — not the feeling, which comes and goes with the weather, but the discipline, the daily decision to stay connected to the source and trust the Vinedresser through a winter that offers nothing to the senses but the cut.

I love that the bones do not assemble themselves, and that even the prophet does not raise them. God tells Ezekiel to prophesy to the bones, to speak the word over the valley of the dead, and Ezekiel does, and there is a noise, and a rattling, and the bones come together, and the sinews and the flesh come on them — and then they lie there, assembled but dead, bodies without breath, which is its own terrible image, the church reassembled and still lifeless. And God has to send the breath, the ruach, the Spirit, and only then do they live and stand on their feet, an exceedingly great army. The prophet's job was to speak the word. The breath was God's to give. That is the whole division of labor in renewal, and the church keeps trying to take both halves. We are called to prophesy to the bones — to speak the word, to abide, to stay faithful in the valley of the dead. We are not able to send the breath. The breath is the sovereign Spirit, and he blows where he wills, and our job is the word and the waiting, not the wind.

I want to be careful, in promising the certainty, not to promise it in the place where it does not apply, because false specificity is the way hopeful books become lying books. The certainty is this: the church of Jesus Christ will not fail, because he promised that the gates of hell would not prevail against it (Matthew 16:18), and he keeps his promises, and the resurrection is the proof that he can keep this one. That is certain. What is not certain — what no promise covers — is that your particular congregation will survive, or that the renewal will come in your lifetime, or in this country, or in any form you would recognize. The promise is to the church, the whole church, the body of Christ across all times and places, not to First Baptist of wherever. Read the promise carefully and you will see that it guarantees the survival of the church and says nothing about the survival of any single lampstand, which is exactly why Christ could promise the church's permanence in one breath and threaten Ephesus with removal in another. Both are true. The church is indestructible; your church is not. And the faith that holds both is the faith that can pour itself out for a particular congregation that may not survive, without either despairing that the church is dying — it is not — or presuming that this church will be spared — it may not. The indestructibility of the whole is the ground of hope. The vulnerability of the part is the call to faithfulness. You labor for the part, knowing it may fall, secure in the whole, knowing it cannot. That is the strange double posture the promise actually creates, and it is far more bracing and far more honest than the cheap version that promises every faithful church a future it was never promised.

That is the certainty. Now the part the church does not want: the renewal is not scheduled, and it is not ours to control, and we may not live to see it. The history of revival is a history of God's freedom — fire that falls when and where he chooses, on the prepared and the unprepared alike, never on demand, never as the reliable output of a method. The Great Awakening came; no committee convened it. The renewals of the church across the centuries have come like weather, not like harvests the church planted on a schedule, and every attempt to manufacture revival by technique has produced emotion and exhaustion and not the thing itself, because the thing itself is the sovereign act of God and not the achievement of the church. We can prepare. We can abide. We can prophesy to the bones and clear the ground and stay rooted and bear what fruit the season allows. We cannot make the spring come. The spring is the Vinedresser's to give, and a church that tries to manufacture it has confused itself with God, which is the oldest error there is and the one underneath all the others.

And here is the weight I promised at the start I would leave and not resolve: you may abide faithfully through the whole of the winter and die before the spring you prepared for. Abraham did. He received the promise of a multitude and died owning a single field and a grave, having seen the promise only from a distance, "having seen them and greeted them from afar" (Hebrews 11:13). Moses led the people forty years toward a land he was permitted to see from a mountain and forbidden to enter; he died on Nebo looking at it. The prophets spoke of a day they did not live to see; "the prophets who prophesied about the grace that was to be yours searched and inquired carefully," and Peter says they were serving not themselves but us, a generation they would never meet (1 Peter 1:10-12). The faithful church of this generation may be, in God's economy, the winter church — the one that abides through the cutting, holds the life of the vine in a few preserved buds, stays rooted through the cold, prophesies to the bones, and dies before the breath comes, leaving the harvest to a generation it will never meet. That is not failure. That is faith. Faith is greeting the promise from afar and dying toward it, planting the tree you will not sit under, prophesying to bones you will not see stand up, abiding through a winter whose spring belongs to someone else.

I want to say something about the relationship between our preparing and God's giving, because the church tends to fall off one side or the other and both falls are deadly. On one side is the church that thinks renewal is entirely up to it — that with the right strategy, the right energy, the right program, it can engineer the spring, and so it strives and strives and exhausts itself and produces a frantic, manufactured imitation of life that burns hot and dies fast, because it was never the breath of God, it was just the church holding its own breath and calling the strain revival. On the other side is the church that thinks renewal is entirely up to God and therefore does nothing — that since the breath is sovereign and cannot be summoned, the church may as well sit still and wait, and so it slides into a fatalism that looks pious and is actually a refusal of the work God did assign. Both are wrong, and the Ezekiel vision corrects both.
