God did not raise the bones without Ezekiel; he told the prophet to prophesy, and the prophet had to actually do it, had to stand in the valley of the dead and speak the word over the corpses, which must have felt absurd, preaching to bones. And God did not need Ezekiel's prophesying to be sufficient in itself; the word arranged the bones but could not breathe into them, and the breath came only when God sent it. So the church's posture is neither striving nor fatalism. It is faithful preparation without the power to guarantee the result — prophesying to the bones, doing the assigned work of the word and the witness and the abiding, and then waiting on a breath we cannot command, refusing both the arrogance that thinks it can manufacture the wind and the sloth that will not do its part because it cannot. We prophesy. God breathes. We do our half knowing it is not enough, and we trust him for the half that only he can do, and the whole thing only works when both halves are honored.

I have to make my own peace with this, and it is not easy, and I will not pretend in the last pages that I have fully made it. I want to see the renewal. I want my church full again, restored, vindicated, in my lifetime, on a timeline I can survive, and I want it partly for God and partly, if I am honest, for me — so that the years of the cutting will have visibly paid off and I will not have to die not knowing. That wanting is the last thing the pruning is cutting out of me. The demand that I personally witness the harvest. The refusal to abide through a winter whose spring I may not see. The insistence that God renew the church on a schedule that rewards my faithfulness where I can watch. I did this, and I am still doing it, and the cut goes deep because this is the deepest root. The Vinedresser is still working on me. He is cutting away my need to see the spring, so that I will abide through the winter for his sake and not for mine, and that cut is the slowest and the most painful of all of them, because it is the cut into the very last thing I was holding back from him — the outcome, the vindication, the proof that it was all worth it. He is asking for that too. He is asking me to plant the tree and trust him for the shade I will never feel, and most days I give it to him with one hand and take it back with the other, and the giving and the taking back is, I have come to think, just what faith looks like from the inside while it is still being formed.

I think often, near the end of these reflections, about the Saturday between the cross and the resurrection, because it is the day the church actually lives in and almost never preaches. We preach Friday, the cross, the death, the cost. We preach Sunday, the resurrection, the victory, the empty tomb. But the disciples lived a Saturday in between, a whole day, and we forget it because the Gospels say almost nothing about it, and they say almost nothing about it because there was almost nothing to say — it was a day of pure loss with no resurrection in sight, a day when everything they had hoped was dead and buried and the stone was rolled across and nothing was happening and no one knew that Sunday was coming. That Saturday is where the declining church lives. We are not on Friday; the worst of the cutting may already be behind us. We are not on Sunday; the renewal has not come and we cannot see it and we have no schedule for it. We are on Saturday, the long day of loss after the cutting and before the rising, the day when the tomb is sealed and faith has nothing to look at but a stone. And the thing about Saturday is that the disciples had no way of knowing it was Saturday. To them it might have been the end, the final day, the day after which there were only more days like it, grief stretching forward without limit. They did not know Sunday was a day away. They could not see it. They only had the loss and the stone and the silence, and they had to live that day without the knowledge that would have made it bearable, which is the knowledge that it was Saturday and not the end. We are in the same position. We do not know whether our church's loss is Saturday or simply the end. We cannot see the Sunday, if there is a Sunday for us. We have only the stone and the silence and the call to keep faith on a day that gives us no evidence the faith is warranted. And the gospel's word for that day is not an argument that Sunday is coming. It is the deeper word that the One who lay in the tomb on Saturday is the same One who walked out of it on Sunday, and that the God who brought resurrection out of the most sealed and silent tomb in history can be trusted with whatever Saturday we are living, even if we cannot see its Sunday, even if its Sunday is not for us but for our children. Saturday faith is the only kind that counts, because anyone can believe on Sunday with the tomb already empty. The faith that holds through Saturday, with the stone still in place and no rising in sight, is the faith of the church in the long decline, and it is the costliest and the truest faith there is.

So I leave you where the pruning leaves the branch: cut, reduced, rooted, and waiting on a Vinedresser who has promised a harvest he has not scheduled. I cannot tell you when the renewal comes. I cannot tell you that you will live to see it. I cannot even tell you, with certainty, that your particular church is being pruned and not removed — that discernment belongs to you and to God and to the slow test of whether you bear fruit through the loss. What I can tell you is what I told you at the beginning, because the whole book has been the long working-out of one sentence: the same blade does both, and the hand on it was pierced for you, and he does not waste the cutting on a branch he means to burn. The knife in your church right now may be the most intimate attention God has paid you in fifty years. Abide through it. Stay rooted. Prophesy to the bones. Bear what fruit the winter allows. Hand the faith to your children. Grieve the losses honestly and pray through the grief. Love the people in front of you and not the crowd you used to have. And leave the spring to the One who owns it.

We do not get the spring. We get the staying. And it turns out the staying — the faithful, rooted, hidden, unrewarded staying through a winter we did not choose and may not survive — is the fruit the Vinedresser was after all along. He never needed the building full. He needed a branch that would hold on through the cold without proof, abide through the cutting without bitterness, and trust the hand that wounded it to bring, in its own time and not in ours, the harvest it promised and we may not see. That branch is the fruit. The staying is the harvest. And the spring, when it comes — for it will come, though I cannot tell you when, and it may not be for us — the spring will only confirm what the winter already proved: that the Vinedresser was never killing his vine. He was loving it, with a knife, the only way a fruitful branch is ever loved.
